newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Key events in Zaire's civil war.
newsitem.headline: Key events in Zaire's civil war.

text.p: Mohamed Sahnoun, the joint U.N.-OAU envoy, announced in South Africa on Thursday that Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila have agreed in principle to meet for talks.
It was not clear when a meeting might be held between the ailing leader and Kabila, whose rebels control half of the sprawling Central African nation.
Here is a chronology of major events in the conflict:

Oct 7: Deputy governor of Zaire's South Kivu province tells 300,000-strong Banyamulenge community -- ethnic Tutsis settled in the region for generations -- to leave Zaire within a week or "be hunted down as rebels". Warning sparks a revolt.
Oct 24: Rebels seize their first major town, Uvira, on northern shore of Lake Tanganyika.
Oct 30: Rebels capture Bukavu, capital of South Kivu province. Bukavu's Roman Catholic archbishop is among the dead.
Nov 1: Rebels and Rwandan soldiers capture Goma, main town in east; about 500 people killed in battles.
Nov 14: Rebels bombard Mugunga, Zaire's biggest refugee camp, with rockets, mortars and heavy artillery for six hours.

Nov 15: Exodus of frightened Rwandan Hutu refugees from Mugunga and other camps. Up to 700,000 refugees return to Rwanda, the remainder flee west with armed Hutu hardliners blamed for 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis there.
Nov 24: Zaire marks 31 years of Mobutu rule; Mobutu is in Europe where he had been since cancer surgery in Switzerland in August.
Nov 28: U.N.-backed military intervention plan fizzles out after exodus home of refugees.
Dec 17: Mobutu flies home to a rousing reception; appoints new armed forces chief and reshuffles government to launch counter-offensive. He returns to France three weeks later.
Jan 20: Government launches much-touted counter-offensive; rebels advance on several fronts, including mineral-rich Shaba province; frustrate army counter-offensive.
Feb 5: Kabila gives Mobutu until Feb 21 to relinquish power or face all-out rebel offensive.
Feb 7: Mobutu returns to Zaire from Europe.
Feb 17: Zaire launches air strikes, bombing rebel-held towns of Bukavu, Shabunda and Walikale.
Feb 18: U.N. Security Council adopts five-point Zaire peace plan proposed by its special envoy Sahnoun.
Feb 19: South Africa tries to broker Zaire peace talks.
Feb 21: Mobutu leaves Zaire for France again.
Feb 28: Organisation of African Unity foreign ministers in Libya urge Zaire truce.
March 3: Zaire's main human rights group speaks of persistent reports of rebels slaughtering Hutus in east.
March 5: Zaire agrees U.N. plan; expels 11 U.N. workers.
March 8 : Rebels say U.N. plan basis for talks.
March 15: Rebels capture Zaire's third city Kisangani.
March 22: Mobutu returns home after fresh cancer treatment in Europe.
March 26: Symbolic handshake between rebels and envoys of Mobutu and Kinshasa authorities at OAU summit in Togo.
March 27: Togo OAU summit on Zaire urges talks, a truce and backing for U.N. peace plan and Sahnoun.
April 2: Mobutu names archrival Etienne Tshisekedi prime minister in place of Kengo wa Dondo; Tshisekedi names government from own loyalists, offers rebels posts. Offer rejected.
April 5: Rebels capture diamond mining centre of Mbuji-Mayi, capital of Kasai province.
April 8: Mobutu declares nationwide state of emergency.
April 9: Rebels capture Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi, capital of southern copper and cobalt province of Shaba.
April 14-15: Tshisekedi supporters close down capital Kinshasa for two days as part of campaign to oust Mobutu.
April 16: South Africa's Nelson Mandela meets Kabila to discuss face-to-face meeting between rebel leader and Mobutu.
April 17: Sahnoun announces agreement in principle for meeting between Mobutu and Kabila.
